headline: In the Heartland Of Old Germany
abstract:
TRAVELING today in what was until recently the German Democratic Republic is an experience at once depressing and fascinating. Depressing, because of the dereliction of the towns, the mood of dazed anxiety and the poor state of tourist services, bureaucratic and not very customer-friendly. Fascinating, because of the bizarre outward symptoms of current revolutionary change (and resistance to it), and the historic and cultural riches of the area from Dresden to Weimar and Eisenach that was the very heartland of the glorious pre-World War I German tradition, so closely linked with Bach, Luther, Goethe, Wagner and others.

Take Leipzig, population 560,000, second city of the former East Germany. It was long a major center of music, literature and publishing, with a great trade fair that still exists. But the surrounding heavy industry, notably the chemical works at Bitterfeld, were allowed by the old regime to grow into such a cesspool of pollution that Leipzig's air is chokingly foul. In the past the city was also exploited for the benefit of East Berlin, deprived of its resources, crippled by neglect; the fierce local resentments against this help to explain why last fall's revolution started there, with the Monday meetings in the Nikolaikirche and the mass rallies on the Karl Marx Platz.

"THE CONSTRUCTED IMAGE," currently on view in the Anthony Giordano Gallery at Dowling College in Oakdale, is a lively, busy exhibition that has considerable breadth.

As a group show concerned with unusual images, it has a fair measure of provocative, disarming and quirky elements readily recognizable. Yet, the dual interest in construction means there is an emphasis, too, on artistic processes that are arbitrary, intuitive and freely inventive.

headline:
DINING OUT;
French Fare in a Banksville Farmhouse
abstract:
WORD of a new chef at La Cremaillere inspired our recent revisits to this rustic farmhouse restaurant run with some success since 1962 by "Robert Meyzen, pere et fils," as the father and son owners style themselves. In addition to the work at the stove, we noted several other changes deserving of mention. Lending an oddly modern feel to the old, unpretentious clapboard farmhouse, the entrance addition now provides space for a dramatic indoor staircase massed with plants and seasonal flowers. 

 Inside, the first room, once the antechamber, retains shelves displaying an attractive collection of provincial china but has been put to good dining use. It is now the most pleasant of La Cremaillere's dining rooms. Tables are spaced at easy intervals and ventilation is excellent, both amenities missing in the older areas; and a pretty country print drapes the windows and covers the shades of sconces giving off a golden glow.

headline:
WINTER IN THE SUN;
1492 and All That: Island Events
abstract:
IN 1492 Christopher Columbus, stubbornly seeking a sea route to China but landing instead on the islands of the Caribbean, thought he had found the mythical Isles of the Blest. While the consequences of that error-ridden voyage are still everywhere palpable in daily life on both sides of the Atlantic, the quincentennial anniversary next year will serve as an occasion for a host of commemorations, celebrations and observances throughout the Caribbean that specifically invoke the spirit of The Discoverer.

The waters of the Caribbean will be crowded with regattas of reproductions of caravels and private boats attempting to trace Columbus's voyage from his sketchy and often intentionally misleading logs. Among others, a crew of Japanese sailors aboard a copy of the Santa Maria will fulfill Columbus's original goal of reaching the East -- though with the help of the Panama Canal -- by sailing from Barcelona to Kobe, Japan, touring the Caribbean along the way.

headline:
DINING OUT;
Shanghai Cuisine Arrives in Larchmont
abstract:
AVOIDING the doldrums in which the once unique Hunan-Sichuan cuisine has been mired -- in most Chinese restaurants the style is now a catchword for whatever the kitchen feels like turning out that's hot with red chili -- Ray's Cafe comes to our rescue. Since it opened seven months ago, this tiny place has attracted a growing clientele delighted with the subtle, ultra-light versions of Shanghai cooking, the cuisine already known for its fresh tastes and natural flavors.

Because of its nearness to many lakes, the marshy land of the Yangtze Delta and the China Sea, the coastal area around Shanghai has been called the land of fish and rice. And diners will find rice in many forms figuring prominently in this cuisine -- in rice noodles, rice wine and rice vinegar, the last two often used as a replacement for soy sauce or salt.

headline: Taking On Mount Kinabalu
abstract:
KINABALU is no mountain for old men. Towering 13,455 feet over the jungles of north Borneo, it is the highest peak in Southeast Asia. But I feel no hesitation, no self-doubt, despite my 43 years. The path is groomed to the top, and when I last hiked to comparable heights -- although it was 10 years ago -- I suffered nothing more than sunburn.

 My wife is perfectly content to stay below, snug in the lavish confines of the Tanjung Aru Beach Hotel, a getaway for expatriates, business executives and other travelers to East Malaysia. There's a pool shimmering before us like a heated oasis. But there's also the mountain, 60 miles into the interior, and I feel its shadow.

headline:
ART REVIEW;
Medical Missionary Work in China
abstract:
IN 1835 the Rev. Peter Parker, M.D., opened a clinic in Canton, China, for the treatment of eye diseases. At the time Western medical practice was virtually unknown in the Far East, where foreign influence was viewed with well-founded suspicion.

Yet, in spite of a limited knowledge of the language and the wide cultural gulf between himself and his patients, Parker's practice flourished and extended well beyond ophthalmology. In the next 20 years his Canton Hospital treated 53,000 people with complaints like kidney stones and leprosy.

headline:
SHOPPER'S WORLD;
Antiques in the Bluegrass
abstract:
AN antiquing tour through Kentucky Bluegrass Country -- an enticing area of horse farms and small towns surrounding Lexington -- means a chance to unearth some great buys in American antiques and, in the bargain, enjoy some of the most beautiful rural countryside anywhere.

The route my wife, Ruth, and I chose last summer began in Lexington, which has plenty of good hotels and motels, and then took in a dozen "down home" towns that are particularly good for antiques. We went from Berea and Lancaster to Frankfort, Paris and Winchester -- all within a circle only 60 miles across. Some of the towns lie along smaller routes and side roads, such as Midway on U.S. Route 62 and Paris on U.S. 68, which afford picturesque views of the horse farms.

Antiques in the Bluegrass AN antiquing tour through Kentucky Bluegrass Country -- an enticing area of horse farms and small towns surrounding Lexington -- means a chance to unearth some great buys in American antiques and, in the bargain, enjoy some of the most beautiful rural countryside anywhere.

The route my wife, Ruth, and I chose last summer began in Lexington, which has plenty of good hotels and motels, and then took in a dozen "down home" towns that are particularly good for antiques. We went from Berea and Lancaster to Frankfort, Paris and Winchester -- all within a circle only 60 miles across. Some of the towns lie along smaller routes and side roads, such as Midway on U.S. Route 62 and Paris on U.S. 68, which afford picturesque views of the horse farms. headline: Germany's Island Fortresses
abstract:
"EVERYTHING here is so settled that one knows exactly everybody's station and standing." So wrote Annette von Droste-Hulshoff, Germany's pre-eminent 19th-century poet, nearly 160 years ago about the Munsterland. She was born and spent most of her life there in largely self-imposed literary seclusion composing ballads and novellas.

Today her portrait is in millions of wallets on the backside of 20-mark banknotes, and it still seems as if nothing has changed in Munsterland, a small Delaware-sized area on the North German Plain between the Dutch border and the bustling coal-mining, steel-making Ruhr Basin.

headline: The Many Worlds of Fun in Japan
abstract:
FOR people who never seem to have time to have fun the Japanese have a lot of amusement options to choose from. In Japan, the landscape is dotted with amusement parks and theme parks, so surely some of this nation's 120 million people must be having at least a little fun. On a recent cross-country trip to five theme parks, I ended up getting a tutorial in cultural osmosis, Japanese style. 

I went to the Kansai region, near Osaka, because ever since reading James Michener's "Sayonara" I'd wanted to see Takarazuka Familyland, home of the Takarazuka Revue, the all-female inspiration for the heroine.

headline: Learning To Stand On Ceremony
abstract:
Sondra Snowdon's first lesson in international business diplomacy and global social protocol came in 1982 when, as a liaison for Citicorp, she was sent to meet a sheik at the airport and he assumed that she was his gift for the weekend. It took her quite a while to convince him that she was not a gift, and when she finally did, it was she who had to apologize so as not to offend.

Today, Ms. Snowdon markets that and other protocol lessons by way of Snowdon's Global Trade and Travel Network, an on-line computer data base that provides global-minded executives a comprehensive protocol-oriented overview of 64 countries. She also offers a worldwide business briefing service by fax and has written two books on the subject (her second, "Snowdon's Official International Protocols," will be published in September by Irwin Professional Publishers). And she does seminars; in annual sessions at the Pierre Hotel she teaches the staff the intricacies of dealing with Japanese guests.

headline: Celebrating A Passion For Roses
abstract:
IT IS almost always worth the trip to visit a collection founded on passion. The passion of Jules Gravereaux, a late 19th-century millionaire and co-founder of the stylish Bon Marche department store in Paris, was for roses -- and it led to the creation in 1894 of the first garden in Europe designed exclusively for them: La Roseraie Departementale de l'Hay-les-Roses, 20 minutes south of Paris by car or 40 minutes by Metro and bus. Not too long after, in 1904, Mr. Gravereaux donated 6,000 roses from l'Hay to the city of Paris to start the rose garden at Bagatelle in the Bois de Boulogne, the city's vast park of over 2,000 acres. The Bagatelle, an 18th century house surrounded by extensive gardens, includes the sumptuous two-acre rose garden. Planted with 11,000 rosebushes of over 850 varieties, it is in bloom throughout the summer.

Mr. Gravereaux and J. C. N. Forestier, the conservator of parks and gardens of Paris and the landscape architect who designed and executed the garden, aimed to put Bagatelle on a par with the best rose gardens of England and Germany and hoped that it would be of general interest to everyone "from the most modest amateur to the most qualified rose specialists," as Mr. Gravereaux wrote.

headline: WEEKEND GETAWAYS; Newport's Great Indoors
abstract:
NARRAGANSETT BAY glowed cornflower blue as I crossed the bridge to Newport, R.I., one windy April weekend. In summer, the city is a mecca for sailors and swimmers, but because it was too early to enjoy the beaches and ocean, I would be exploring Newport indoors before the crowds arrived. 

 I had made reservations at the Sanford-Covell Villa Marina, a three-story stick style house with a decorative arts interior on Narragansett Bay in the gaslighted colonial Point neighborhood, less than a mile from the center of town. The house, on the National Register of Historic Places, has a magnificent three-story entryway, open from floor to ceiling and stenciled in floral and geometric designs. The bayside parlor contained two baby grand pianos and crystal decanters of port and sherry. I felt comfortable right away, as if I were visiting my grandmother's house -- if my grandmother had been rich.

abstract: AMERICAS CANADA: ECONOMY STALLS Canada's economy stalled in February, as output dropped 0.1 percent after a 0.3 percent rise in January, but the decline was only half as bad as economists had predicted. Manufacturing led gross domestic product down, with a 0.9 percent drop, and production of electrical and electronic equipment fell 9.1 percent, the worst reversal in 40 years. "Major customers, primarily from the United States, continued to curtail spending, sparking significant production cutbacks and layoffs by key Canadian producers," said Statistics Canada, the government's reporting agency. Gains in construction, mining and forestry partly offset the decline in manufacturing.

headline: BUSINESS DIGEST
abstract: Home Speculation Unseats Investment in Stocks  In several metropolitan areas where the real estate market is hot, rapidly rising sales prices are luring a growing number of ordinary people into buying and selling residences they will never occupy.    According to LoanPerformance Inc., about 8.5 percent of mortgages in the first 11 months of last year were taken out by people who do not plan to live in the homes themselves, up from 5.8 percent in 2000. [Page A1.]    No Allied Domecq-Pernod Deal  Shares of Pernod Ricard declined after it was learned that the company has given up on the idea of taking over Allied Domecq. An out-and-out purchase by the French company was never likely: Pernod's market value, at just more than $10 billion, is slightly smaller than Allied's. Making a joint bid with another spirits company could theoretically give Pernod the mass to get a deal done. But finding such a partner is tricky. Market Place. [C11.]    Continental Unions Agree to Cuts  Continental Airlines reached tentative agreements with its unions on $500 million in annual savings, the fifth major airline to obtain cuts from all its workers. [C9.]    Senate Discussing Bankruptcy Bill  Legislation sought by banks and credit card companies to make it more difficult for consumers to discharge their debts in personal bankruptcy made its way to the Senate. [C2.]    Law Partnerships More Elusive  Making partner at big law firms is getting more difficult. The number of equity partners at law firms grew 2.5 percent last year, down from 4.5 percent five years ago. [C3.]    Ford Sued for Lending Practices  Ford Motor Credit, which makes car loans, is being sued on charges that the company's lending practices allow dealers to discriminate against minorities. [C2.]    China Goes to Latin America for Oil  China is shopping for oil. China has signed accords with Venezuela, invested in largely untapped markets like Peru and explored possibilities in Bolivia and Colombia. [C6.]    A Smaller Quarterly Loss at Fiat  Sergio Marchionne, left, Fiat's chief executive, has been piecing together a turnaround that has resulted in factory closings, management layoffs and the introduction of more than a dozen new or redesigned models. As a result, Fiat's fourth-quarter loss shrank to 374 million euros, or $495 million, from 1.1 billion euros in the final quarter of 2003. Sales were little changed at 12.5 billion euros. [C6.]    Givenchy Names a Designer  Riccardo Tisci was named Givenchy's creative director for women's wear. [C6.]    Couple Wins Suit Against Merrill  An arbitration panel has awarded a Florida couple more than $1 million for losses they claimed were caused by Merrill Lynch's fraudulent research. [C9.]    Hint of Inflation Cuts Bond Prices  With a whiff of inflation in the air, Treasury prices fell. The yield on the 10-year note jumped to 4.38 percent. [C11.]    The Dow Jones industrials declined 75.37 points, to 10,766.23; the S.&P. 500 dropped 7.77 points, to 1,203.60; and the Nasdaq composite index fell 13.68 points, to 2,051.72. [C11.]    The Pros and Cons of Upgrades  A modified Dear John letter about upgrades on Continental Airlines draws both pros and cons. Joe Sharkey: On the Road. [C8.]

headline: Kicks, Off Route 46
abstract: FOR a restaurant in a densely populated section of the nation's most densely populated state, the Fat Kat is about as far from the beaten track as you can get.    Its address is Main Street in this central Bergen County industrial town, just a block south of the pounding night-and-day traffic of Route 46, but it has never had much prospect of walk-in customers. In fact, if you're walking, you may want to give a wide berth to the place next door, surrounded by a chain-link fence with a ''Beware of Dog'' sign. Other neighbors include an automatic laundry, a hardware store and a miscellany of Depression-era frame houses.

headline: Taking Fashion to the Streets
abstract: TIERED skirts, glass beads, supersize shades and curly-toed slippers fit for Scheherazade: the jumble of wares massed inside the stalls at the Howard Street market in downtown Manhattan left Rachel Cohen giddy. Pawing though an assortment of crazily embroidered peasant skirts last week, Ms. Cohen, a 27-year-old physiotherapist from Jerusalem, said her forays into such bazaars are usually desultory, a mix of shopping and plenty of unfocused roaming. But Howard Street was different.      ''Shopping here is an anthropological experience,'' she said with a glance at the crowd. ''Here you can find something authentic, a bit of real city life.''

headline: Teenager Uses Upset of Roddick to Motivate
abstract: It figures that Sania Mirza would find inspiration in the first-round upset of Andy Roddick by Luxembourg's Gilles Muller. Mirza, like Muller, knows how it feels to carry a racket bag sagging with the weight of a country's expectations.     Mirza is ranked No. 42 in the world. She is the first woman from India to grace the top 100. After weathering the wind and Maria Elena Camerin, 6-4, 1-6, 6-4, in a second-round match yesterday afternoon at Armstrong Stadium, Mirza said Muller's monumental victory made her feel ''that you can do it, too, like a lot of people out there who are coming out of the odds.''

headline: BUSINESS DIGEST
abstract: In Storm's Wake, Turmoil in Energy Market Spurs Release of Strategic Petroleum Stocks  The nation's largest energy center was still reeling four days after Hurricane Katrina slammed into the Gulf of Mexico, crippling gasoline supplies in some pockets of the country. In the face of the turmoil, the government stepped up its release of strategic oil stocks to refiners. [Page C1.]    All across the country dealers posted eye-popping gasoline prices yesterday, reflecting panic in both dealers and consumers not seen since the days immediately after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. [C1.]    Soaring gasoline prices and fears over gasoline supplies are causing Labor Day weekend travelers to calculate how much the trip will cost by car, whether it is cheaper to fly and how easy it will be to fill up. [C1.]    Prosecutors Sue Hedge Fund Company  Federal prosecutors sued the Bayou Funds, accusing the Connecticut hedge fund company and securities firm of directing a fraud lasting for years that drew in more than $300 million in investors' money. [C1.]    Novartis Offers Chiron a Buyout Deal  The Swiss pharmaceutical company Novartis said it had offered to pay $4.5 billion to take over Chiron, a troubled American biotechnology company. Novartis already owns 42 percent of Chiron, the world's second-largest producer of flu vaccines. In 2004, British regulators forced the closing of Chiron's factory in Liverpool because of quality problems, which led to a flu vaccine shortfall in the United States last year. [C3.]    German Executive Takes On a Rebuilding Job  In May, three years after being forced out of the media giant Bertelsmann, Thomas Middelhoff took on one of the most grueling corporate salvage jobs in Germany, at the troubled department store and mail-order chain KarstadtQuelle. ''There was a need for immediate action,'' he said. [C1.]    Chicago Case Said to Link Stun Gun to Heart Disturbance  A shock from a Taser stun gun caused a teenager in Chicago to go into ventricular fibrillation, a usually fatal heart disturbance, according to a letter published in The New England Journal of Medicine. headline: Metro Briefing | New York: Bronx: 28 Charged In Cigarette Smuggling
abstract: The police have arrested 28 men -- many of them Jordanian nationals -- accused of selling untaxed and sometimes counterfeit-label cigarettes to store owners in the Bronx, Yonkers and Manhattan, the police said yesterday. The scheme involved buying cigarettes from Suffolk County's Shinnecock and Poospatuck reservations, where they are not taxed, and from cigarette counterfeiters based in China, and reselling them to bodegas for half the cost of legitimately taxed cigarettes, the police said. The enterprise is believed to have generated approximately $10 million in profits since the investigation began in 2003, the police said. Approximately $500,000 was sent to unknown recipients in Amman, Jordan, by way of crew members of Royal Jordanian Airlines, according to the Bronx district attorney's office. Those arrested are charged collectively with 1,237 counts of money laundering, possession of forged instruments, trademark counterfeiting and other offenses. Investigators seized or bought, through undercover officers, more than 15,000 cartons of cigarettes and seized more than $700,000, the police said.  Michael Wilson (NYT)

headline: SPORTS BRIEFING
abstract: N.B.A.       $75 Million Pact for Yao       Yao Ming, the Houston Rockets' 7-foot-6 center, signed a five-year contract worth more than $75 million yesterday, keeping him with the team through the 2010-11 season. The extension was the maximum allowed under the N.B.A.'s new labor deal.     The contract, announced in a conference call, will be 25 percent of the salary cap, meaning the first year will be worth $12.5 million. Yao, a three-time All-Star, has a year left on his rookie contract, which will pay him more than $5.5 million next season.

headline: World Briefing | Asia: Typhoon Lashes Taiwan And Threatens China

The storm cut power lines and uprooted trees before crossing into Fujian Province in China, bringing heavy winds and strong rain that knocked out power to large parts of the provincial capital, Fuzhou.

The treaty became truly effective only after 1992, when France and China signed it. headline: Thinking the Unthinkable on Iran
abstract: To the Editor:     After so many claims that nuclear weapons in the hands of mad ayatollahs would present an unacceptable risk for Israel, the Middle East, the United States and the rest of the world, it is sobering to read Barry R. Posen's balanced argument.      The Iranian regime has issued some outrageous statements and has used deception and cheating for covering its nuclear program, but that does not make it irrational or indeed suicidal.

headline: Paid Notice: Deaths   HEILIGMAN, DR. SOL J.
abstract: HEILIGMAN--Dr. Sol J. We are profoundly saddened by the passing of our long time resident and friend, Sol. He and his beloved late wife Shirley were staunch supporters of our community for over 30 years. He will be greatly missed. Sedgewood Club Associates China Barrett Association     HEILIGMAN--Dr. Sol J. After a life-long friendship of 72 years, I bid a sad farewell to my dear friend, Sol. It was a great ride, but it ended too soon. Fare thee well, Sol. Gene Grant     HEILIGMAN--Dr. Sol J. Age 90, on June 24, 2006, at his country home on China Lake, Carmel, NY. Beloved husband of the late Shirley Sperans Heiligman, devoted stepfather of Andrew (Nan), and Tom (Randy), loving uncle of Janet Heiligman, and brother-in-law of Phyllis (Parker). He was born in Fort Wayne, IN. At an early age, his widowed mother brought him and his four siblings to New York. He graduated from CCNY (B.S.) in 1937, and the University of Michigan (Doctor of Dental Surgery) in 1941. In WWII, he served with distinction as a Captain in a Combat Artillery Regiment in Europe. After the war, he volunteered as a Dental Surgeon on the ship ''Project Hope'' in Nicaragua for several seasons. He then embarked on a long and distinguished career in Dental Medicine in New York City, specializing in Periodontia. In recent years, he was a respected volunteer in the Ichthyology Dept. of the American Museum of Natural History. An avid sportsman, he loved tennis, skiing, horseback riding, canoeing and wilderness camping. A bachelor until he was 52, he was married to Shirley Sperans Karsch for 35 years, until her untimely passing in 2003. Funeral services at Frank E. Campbell, 1076 Madison Avenue/81st Street, at 4pm, on Thursday, June 29. In lieu of flowers, contributions may be made to Marymount College, East 71st Street, NY, NY in loving memory of Dr. Sol and Shirley Heiligman.

headline: Searching China, Heart on Sleeve
abstract: The opening shot of the new Zhang Yimou picture is as spectacular as anything in ''Hero'' or ''House of Flying Daggers.'' An old man broods on a black crag, the silver sea churning before him. Sea gulls twist in the gray sky above, dodging shafts of sunlight that fall like bamboo spears drained of their chlorophyll. A little uncanny (has it been digitally manipulated?) and a whole lot clichéd, the tableau speaks of melancholy graced by a pale sliver of hope. You'd roll your eyes if they weren't so dazzled.      Yet there's no arguing with the calm of the composition or the splendor of the color (credit the cinematographer, Zhao Xiaoding), and its very simplicity, verging on the simple-minded, strips down feeling to its essence. Vulnerable, corny and disarmingly frank, a film in which people don't just weep but slobber and moan, ''Riding Alone for Thousands of Miles'' drives melodrama right off the map. Cynics are in for a very long haul.

headline: Japan Wages Fell in March
abstract: Wages in Japan fell for a fourth month in March, signaling that growth in consumer spending will be limited. Monthly wages, including overtime and bonuses, fell 0.4 percent after dropping 1 percent in February, the labor ministry said. In China, manufacturing activity expanded at the fastest pace in more than two years in April, according to a survey of purchasing managers. The Purchasing Managers’ Index rose to 58.6 from 56.1 in March, the statistics bureau said. That is the highest since the index started in January 2005.

headline: Batteries Included in New Travel Restrictions
abstract: BATTERY RESTRICTIONS Beginning Tuesday, airline passengers cannot pack any loose lithium batteries in checked bags, though the batteries are permitted if contained within laptops, cellphones or other electronic devices, according to a new rule by the Transportation Department. The department said that loose lithium batteries can short-circuit and create a fire hazard in cargo holds. The new rule also limits to two the number of large-size spare lithium batteries that may be brought on in carry-on bags, but a department spokeswoman says that restriction applies mostly to professional and industrial-use batteries and does not affect most lithium batteries used in consumer electronics like laptops and cellphones.

headline: Shanghai Cancels Art Exhibition
abstract: An exhibition of works by the artist Zhang Huan, right, was canceled by Shanghai’s local government just before it was to open this week at the Shanghai Art Museum. The Shanghai Cultural Bureau, which oversees the museum, declined to comment on Friday, as did museum officials and Mr. Zhang. But people in Shanghai closely involved with the exhibition said government officials seemed to be troubled by some of his installation works, including two sculptures, “Giant 1” and “Giant 2,” 16-foot-tall deformed creatures with human faces and body parts made from cowhide. The same people said that museum officials were still negotiating with the government and that they hoped that it would allow the show to open within a month. China regularly censors or closes art shows, particularly if they depict work that is overtly political or has sexual or violent themes. But in recent years the government has allowed many formerly banned artists to exhibit.
